questions.q: Which of these is a root of x⁴ + 4 = 0?
questions.x: (1 + i)² = 2i and (2i)² = −4, so (1 + i)⁴ + 4 = 0. In fact x⁴ + 4 = (x² − 2x + 2)(x² + 2x + 2), with roots ±1 ± i. By contrast (√2 i)⁴ = 4 and (2i)⁴ = 16.

questions.q: What is √(7 + 4√3)?
questions.x: Look for (p + √q)² = p² + q + 2p√q = 7 + 4√3: p = 2, q = 3 works (4 + 3 = 7 and 2·2√3 = 4√3). Check: (2 + √3)² = 7 + 4√3, while (1 + 2√3)² = 13 + 4√3. Taking roots term by term (√7 + √4) is the usual slip.

questions.q: A function satisfies f(x) + 2f(1/x) = 3x for every x ≠ 0. What is f(2)?
questions.x: x = 2 gives f(2) + 2f(½) = 6, and x = ½ gives f(½) + 2f(2) = 3/2. Substituting f(½) = 3/2 − 2f(2) into the first: f(2) + 3 − 4f(2) = 6, so f(2) = −1. Check: f(x) = 2/x − x satisfies the equation and f(2) = −1.

questions.q: f(x) = 2x − 1. Which expression equals f(f(f(x)))?
questions.x: f(f(x)) = 2(2x − 1) − 1 = 4x − 3, and f(4x − 3) = 2(4x − 3) − 1 = 8x − 7. Check x = 1: f(1) = 1, so f(f(f(1))) = 1 = 8 − 7. 6x − 3 is 3f(x), a product, not a composition.

questions.q: lim(n→∞) (1 + 1/n)^(n + 5) equals:
questions.x: (1 + 1/n)^(n + 5) = (1 + 1/n)ⁿ · (1 + 1/n)⁵. The first factor tends to e and the second to 1⁵ = 1, so the limit is e.

questions.q: a + b + c = 0. What is |[[a, b, c], [b, c, a], [c, a, b]]|?
questions.x: Add columns 2 and 3 to column 1 (the value does not change): every entry of column 1 becomes a + b + c = 0, so the determinant is 0. Check a = 1, b = −1, c = 0: 1(0 − 1) + 1(1 − 0) + 0 = 0.

questions.q: α and β are the roots of x² − 2x + 4 = 0. Which equation has roots α + 1/β and β + 1/α?
questions.x: α + β = 2 and αβ = 4. New sum = (α + β) + (α + β)/(αβ) = 2 + 1/2 = 5/2; new product = αβ + 2 + 1/(αβ) = 4 + 2 + 1/4 = 25/4. So x² − (5/2)x + 25/4 = 0, i.e. 4x² − 10x + 25 = 0. Leaving out the middle term 2 in the product gives 17/4 and the 17 option.

questions.q: The parabola y = ax² + bx + c passes through (0, 3), (1, 2) and (−1, 6). What is its vertex?
questions.x: c = 3; then a + b = −1 and a − b = 3, so a = 1, b = −2 and y = x² − 2x + 3 = (x − 1)² + 2. The vertex is (1, 2). Check: (2, 3) lies on the curve too but y there is 3, above the minimum 2.

questions.q: a and b are unequal constants. In the partial fractions of x/((x − a)(x − b)), what is the coefficient of 1/(x − a)?
questions.x: Cover up x − a and put x = a in what is left: a/(a − b). The other coefficient is b/(b − a), and the two add to 1, matching the x term on top. Check with a = 2, b = 3: x/((x − 2)(x − 3)) = −2/(x − 2) + 3/(x − 3), and a/(a − b) = −2.

questions.q: For which value of x are x + 1, 2x + 1 and 4x − 1 consecutive terms of an A.P.?
questions.x: The middle term is the arithmetic mean of its neighbours: 2(2x + 1) = (x + 1) + (4x − 1), so 4x + 2 = 5x and x = 2. Check: the terms are 3, 5, 7 with difference 2.

questions.q: How many of the integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by neither 2 nor 5?
questions.x: Divisible by 2: 50; by 5: 20; by both (by 10): 10. So 50 + 20 − 10 = 60 are divisible by 2 or 5, and 100 − 60 = 40 are divisible by neither. Check: in each block of 10 only the units digits 1, 3, 7, 9 qualify, 4 × 10 = 40. Forgetting to add back the 10 gives 30.

questions.q: What is the value of 0! + 1! + 2! + 3!?
questions.x: 0! = 1, 1! = 1, 2! = 2 and 3! = 6, so the sum is 1 + 1 + 2 + 6 = 10. Taking 0! = 0 gives 9.

questions.q: The coefficient of x² in the expansion of (1 + x)(1 − x)⁴ is:
questions.x: (1 − x)⁴ = 1 − 4x + 6x² − …; x² comes from 1 × 6x² and x × (−4x), so the coefficient is 6 − 4 = 2. Check: (1 + x)(1 − x)⁴ = (1 − x²)(1 − x)³, giving 3 − 1 = 2.

questions.q: For angles where it is defined, (sec²θ − 1) cos²θ simplifies to:
questions.x: sec²θ − 1 = tan²θ, and tan²θ · cos²θ = (sin²θ/cos²θ) · cos²θ = sin²θ. Stopping at sec²θ − 1 = tan²θ gives the tan²θ slip.

questions.q: For every x, sin 4x − sin 2x can be written as:
questions.x: sin C − sin D = 2 cos((C + D)/2) sin((C − D)/2) = 2 cos 3x sin x. 2 sin 3x cos x is the form for sin 4x + sin 2x.

questions.q: The function f(x) = sin x + cos x is:
questions.x: f(−x) = −sin x + cos x, which is neither f(x) nor −f(x). For example f(π/4) = √2 but f(−π/4) = 0. A sum of an odd and an even function (both non-zero) is neither.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, A = 45°, B = 60° and c = √3 + 1. What is a?
The graph of y = sec⁻¹x has no points in the vertical strip:
questions.x: sec⁻¹x is defined only for |x| ≥ 1, because sec θ never lies strictly between −1 and 1. So the graph has two branches, x ≤ −1 and x ≥ 1, with nothing in −1 < x < 1; 0 to π is its range, not a gap in x.

questions.q: The solutions of sin θ cos θ = 1/4 in the interval 0 ≤ θ < π are:
questions.x: sin θ cos θ = ½ sin 2θ, so sin 2θ = 1/2 with 0 ≤ 2θ < 2π, giving 2θ = π/6 or 5π/6, so θ = π/12 or 5π/12. The pair π/6, 5π/6 solves sin θ = 1/2 instead.

questions.q: Which of these functions has no Maclaurin series?
questions.x: A Maclaurin series needs f and all its derivatives at x = 0. ln x is not defined at 0, so it has none (it is expanded about x = 1 instead); ln(1 + x) is fine at 0.

questions.q: If f(x) = x eˣ, what is f″(0)?
questions.x: f′(x) = eˣ + x eˣ = (x + 1)eˣ, and f″(x) = eˣ + (x + 1)eˣ = (x + 2)eˣ, so f″(0) = 2. Stopping at f′(0) gives 1.

questions.q: ∫ sin⁻¹x/√(1 − x²) dx, for |x| < 1, equals:
questions.x: Put u = sin⁻¹x, du = dx/√(1 − x²): ∫u du = u²/2 + C = ½(sin⁻¹x)² + C. Without the ½, differentiating (sin⁻¹x)² gives twice the integrand.

questions.q: ∫ x² cos x dx equals:
o: x² sin x + 2x cos x − 2 sin x + C
x² sin x − 2x cos x + 2 sin x + C
x² sin x + 2x cos x + 2 sin x + C
x² sin x − 2x sin x + C
questions.x: First parts: x² sin x − ∫2x sin x dx; then ∫2x sin x dx = −2x cos x + 2 sin x. So the result is x² sin x + 2x cos x − 2 sin x + C. Differentiating it back gives 2x sin x + x² cos x − 2x sin x + 2 cos x − 2 cos x = x² cos x.

questions.q: A radioactive sample decays at a rate proportional to the amount present. 100 g falls to 80 g in one day. How much is left after three days?
questions.x: N = 100e^(−kt) with e^(−k) = 0.8, so N(3) = 100 × 0.8³ = 51.2 g. Losing 20 g every day gives 40 g; 64 g is the amount after two days.

questions.q: What is the area of the triangle formed by the lines y = x, y = −x and y = 3?
questions.x: The vertices are (0, 0), (3, 3) and (−3, 3): base 6 at height 3, so the area is ½ × 6 × 3 = 9. Forgetting the ½ gives 18.

questions.q: For any angle θ, what is the distance from the point (cos θ, sin θ) to the line x cos θ + y sin θ − 3 = 0?
questions.x: Distance = |cos²θ + sin²θ − 3|/√(cos²θ + sin²θ) = |1 − 3|/1 = 2. The point is on the unit circle and the line is 3 from O along the same normal, so they are 2 apart.

questions.q: The tangents to the parabola y² = 4x at the two ends of its latus rectum meet at which point?
questions.x: The ends are (1, 2) and (1, −2). The tangents are 2y = 2(x + 1) and −2y = 2(x + 1), i.e. y = x + 1 and y = −x − 1, which meet at (−1, 0), a point of the directrix x = −1.

questions.q: Which point lies on the hyperbola x²/4 − y²/9 = 1?
For non-zero vectors a and b, when is |a + b|² = |a|² + |b|²?
o: When a and b are perpendicular
When a and b are parallel
questions.x: |a + b|² = |a|² + 2a · b + |b|², so the equality holds exactly when a · b = 0, i.e. a ⊥ b. This is the vector form of Pythagoras' theorem.

questions.q: For vectors a, b and c, what does a · (b × c) = 0 tell us?
o: The vectors all have the same length
The vectors are all unit vectors
questions.x: |a · (b × c)| is the volume of the parallelepiped on a, b and c. Zero volume means the three vectors lie in one plane. Mutually perpendicular non-zero vectors give a non-zero volume.

questions.q: For a real gas, (p + a/V²)(V − b) = RT, where p is the pressure and V the volume. The dimensions of the constant a are:
questions.x: Only like quantities can be added, so a/V² has the dimensions of pressure: a = pV² = [ML⁻¹T⁻²][L⁶] = [ML⁵T⁻²]. Dividing by V² instead of multiplying gives [ML⁻⁷T⁻²]; [L³] is the dimension of b.

questions.q: A rectangle measures 12.5 cm by 4.0 cm. Its perimeter and its area, each written to the correct number of significant figures, are:
questions.x: Perimeter = 2(12.5 + 4.0) = 33.0 cm: in addition the answer keeps one decimal place, as the data do (the 2 is exact). Area = 12.5 × 4.0 = 50 cm², limited to two significant figures by 4.0, so 5.0 × 10¹ cm². Dropping the final zero of the perimeter is the common slip.

questions.q: Vector P = 2î + mĵ is perpendicular to vector Q = 3î − 6ĵ. The value of m is:
questions.x: Perpendicular vectors have P · Q = 0: (2)(3) + (m)(−6) = 6 − 6m = 0, so m = 1. Dropping the minus sign of −6ĵ gives m = −1.

questions.q: According to Newton's third law, the action and reaction forces between two bodies:
o: Act on the same body and cancel each other
Act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other
Are equal only when the bodies are at rest
questions.x: Action and reaction are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and act on different bodies, so they cannot cancel. Thinking they act on the same body and cancel is the common misconception.

questions.q: A car moves at 20 m s⁻¹ for 10 s, stands still for 10 s, then moves at 10 m s⁻¹ for 20 s in the same direction. Its average speed for the whole 40 s is:
questions.x: Distance = 20 × 10 + 0 + 10 × 20 = 400 m in 40 s, so average speed = 10 m s⁻¹. Averaging the two speeds gives 15 m s⁻¹; leaving out the 10 s stop gives 400/30 = 40/3 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A pendulum bob is released from rest at a point 0.8 m higher than its lowest point. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its speed at the lowest point is:
questions.x: PE lost = KE gained: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) = √16 = 4 m s⁻¹; the mass cancels. Forgetting the square root gives 16 m s⁻¹; dropping the 2 gives √8 = 2√2 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A body moves at constant speed in a circle. The centripetal force on it does no work because:
o: It is balanced by an equal outward force
It is always perpendicular to the body's velocity
It is always parallel to the body's velocity
The body's kinetic energy is zero
questions.x: Work = Fd cos θ, and the centripetal force always acts along the radius, at 90° to the velocity, so cos 90° = 0 and no work is done; the speed and kinetic energy stay constant. A force parallel to the velocity would change the speed.

questions.q: A car moves at 15 m s⁻¹ on wheels of radius 0.25 m that roll without slipping. Taking π ≈ 3.14, each wheel turns at about:
questions.x: ω = v/r = 15/0.25 = 60 rad s⁻¹ = 60/(2 × 3.14) ≈ 9.55 rev s⁻¹ ≈ 573 rev min⁻¹. Dividing by π instead of 2π gives 1146; 60 is the value in rad s⁻¹, not rev min⁻¹.

questions.q: Two solid spheres of the same radius, with densities 3000 kg m⁻³ and 2000 kg m⁻³, fall through a liquid of density 1000 kg m⁻³. The ratio of their terminal velocities is:
questions.x: With upthrust, v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/9η, so for equal radii v_t ∝ (ρ − σ): (3000 − 1000) : (2000 − 1000) = 2 : 1. Ignoring the upthrust gives 3000 : 2000 = 3 : 2.

questions.q: The bob of a simple pendulum, of mass m, is displaced so that the string makes an angle θ with the vertical. The force that pulls the bob back towards its mean position is:
questions.x: Resolve the weight: mg cos θ acts along the string (balanced, with the centripetal part, by the tension) and mg sin θ acts along the arc towards the mean position. This tangential part is the restoring force.

questions.q: According to the principle of superposition, when two waves overlap at a point, the resultant displacement there is the:
o: Product of the displacements due to the separate waves
Vector sum of the displacements due to the separate waves
Larger of the two separate displacements
Difference of the two amplitudes, whatever the phases
questions.x: Superposition: the resultant displacement at each instant is the vector (signed) sum of the individual displacements. Whether this gives reinforcement or cancellation depends on the phases.

questions.q: Which of these cannot travel through a vacuum?
questions.x: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium to carry its vibrations. Light, radio waves and X-rays are electromagnetic waves and travel through empty space.

questions.q: In a single-slit diffraction pattern, the central bright band, compared with each of the other bright bands, is:
o: About half as wide and fainter
The same width and the same brightness
About twice as wide and much brighter
questions.x: The central band stretches from the first minimum on one side to the first minimum on the other, sin θ = ±λ/a, while each side band lies between neighbouring minima. So the central band is about twice as wide, and it carries most of the light.

questions.q: Doctors look inside a patient's stomach with an endoscope. The endoscope carries light and the image along:
o: A narrow hollow metal tube with mirrors
questions.x: An endoscope uses flexible bundles of optical fibres: one bundle carries light in by total internal reflection, and a coherent bundle carries the image back out.

questions.q: In each cycle a real engine takes 1200 J of heat from a reservoir at 600 K and rejects 900 J to a reservoir at 300 K. What is the total entropy change of the two reservoirs per cycle?
questions.x: Hot reservoir: −1200/600 = −2 J K⁻¹; cold reservoir: +900/300 = +3 J K⁻¹; total +1 J K⁻¹. A positive total fits an irreversible engine (its efficiency 25% is below the Carnot value 50%). Adding the magnitudes gives 5 J K⁻¹.

questions.q: In each cycle, a heat engine:
o: Turns all the heat it takes from the source into work
Takes heat from the cold sink and gives it to the hot source
Takes heat from a hot source, turns part of it into work and gives the rest to a cold sink
Does work without taking in any heat
questions.x: A heat engine works between two reservoirs: it absorbs Q₁ from the hot source, does work W, and rejects Q₂ = Q₁ − W to the cold sink. Turning all the heat into work is forbidden by the second law.

questions.q: Charges of +2 μC and −3 μC are 30 cm apart in oil of relative permittivity 2.5. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the force between them is:
questions.x: In air F = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ × 3 × 10⁻⁶/0.09 = 0.6 N; in the oil F = 0.6/2.5 = 0.24 N, attractive because the charges are unlike. Multiplying by εr gives 1.5 N.

questions.q: The volt, the unit of potential difference, is equal to:
questions.x: Potential difference is work done per unit charge, V = W/q, so 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹. J s⁻¹ is the watt.

questions.q: A battery of emf 6 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is being charged by a charger that drives a current of 2 A into its positive terminal. The p.d. across the battery's terminals during charging is:
questions.x: During charging the current flows against the emf, so the charger must supply the emf plus the internal drop: V = E + Ir = 6 + 2 × 0.5 = 7 V. Subtracting Ir, as when the battery is discharging, gives 5 V.

questions.q: Ohm's law (the current through a conductor is proportional to the p.d. across it) holds for a metal wire only if:
o: Its length is less than one metre
The current flows for less than one second
The p.d. across it is less than 1 V
Its temperature and other physical conditions stay the same
questions.x: Ohm's law, V ∝ I, holds only while the temperature and other physical conditions of the conductor stay constant. Heating a wire changes its resistance; the wire's length and the time the current flows are not conditions of the law.

questions.q: For a long straight current-carrying wire, the magnetic field B is plotted against 1/r, where r is the distance from the wire. The graph is:
o: A straight line through the origin
A straight line with a negative gradient
questions.x: B = (μ₀I/2π) × (1/r), so B is directly proportional to 1/r: a straight line through the origin with gradient μ₀I/2π. B against r itself would be the falling curve.

questions.q: The back emf in the armature of a DC motor, running on a fixed supply, is greatest when the motor:
o: Has just been switched on from rest
Is heavily loaded and slows down
Runs at its highest speed with no mechanical load
questions.x: The back emf is the generator emf of the rotating armature, so it is proportional to the speed. It is largest at the highest speed (no load) and zero when the armature is at rest.

questions.q: In a series RLC circuit connected to an AC supply, the rms voltages across the resistor, inductor and capacitor are 30 V, 70 V and 30 V. The rms supply voltage is:
questions.x: VL and VC are 180° apart, so their net is 70 − 30 = 40 V, at 90° to VR: V = √(30² + 40²) = 50 V. Adding all three as numbers gives 130 V; 70 V adds VR to the net reactive voltage.

questions.q: In a body-centred cubic unit cell, one atom sits at each of the 8 corners of the cube and one atom at its centre. Each corner atom is shared equally by 8 neighbouring unit cells. The number of atoms belonging to one unit cell is:
questions.x: Each corner atom contributes 1/8 to the cell: 8 × 1/8 = 1, and the centre atom belongs wholly to the cell, giving 1 + 1 = 2. Counting every atom fully gives 9; forgetting the centre atom gives 1.

questions.q: LEDs that give red, yellow and green light are made from different semiconductor compounds. The colour of the light from an LED depends mainly on:
o: The energy gap of the semiconductor material
The size of the current through it
The value of the series resistor
questions.x: Each photon is emitted when an electron falls across the energy gap, so the photon energy, and hence its wavelength and colour, is set by the gap of the material (a larger gap gives a shorter wavelength). The current only changes the brightness.

questions.q: A photovoltaic (solar) cell:
o: Emits light when a current is passed through it
Needs a reverse-bias battery to produce a current
Converts light energy directly into electrical energy without any external bias
questions.x: Light makes electron-hole pairs at the junction, and the junction's own field separates them, so the cell itself acts as a source of e.m.f. Emitting light is what an LED does; a photodiode, not a solar cell, is used with reverse bias.

questions.q: The position of a 0.1 kg ball is known to within 1 mm. Using Δx Δp ≈ h with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the uncertainty in its speed is about:
questions.x: Δv = h/(mΔx) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.1 × 1 × 10⁻³) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁰ m s⁻¹, far too small to notice, which is why the principle matters only for tiny particles. 6.63 × 10⁻³¹ is Δp (not divided by the mass); taking Δx as 1 m gives 6.63 × 10⁻³³.

questions.q: The target of an X-ray tube is usually made of tungsten and is often cooled with circulating oil or water. This is because:
o: The X-rays themselves heat the target strongly
Nearly all the energy of the electrons hitting the target turns into heat
Cooling increases the energy of the X-ray photons
questions.x: Only about 1% of the electrons' kinetic energy becomes X-rays; the rest becomes heat in the target, so a high-melting-point metal like tungsten is used and it is cooled. The X-ray photon energies are set by the accelerating voltage, not by cooling.

questions.q: Energy is released both when very light nuclei fuse and when very heavy nuclei split. This is because in both processes:
o: The total number of nucleons increases
The binding energy per nucleon of the products is greater than that of the reactants
The binding energy per nucleon of the products is smaller
questions.x: The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve peaks near iron-56. Fusing light nuclei and splitting heavy ones both move towards the peak, so the products are more tightly bound and the extra binding energy is released, with a matching loss of mass. Nucleon number is conserved.

questions.q: A free neutron decays as n → p + e⁻ + X. Conservation of charge and of lepton number requires the particle X to be:
questions.x: Charge already balances (0 = +1 − 1), so X is neutral. Lepton number is 0 on the left, and the electron has +1, so X must have −1: an antilepton, the electron antineutrino. A neutrino would give a total lepton number of +2; a positron is charged.

questions.q: Chlorine is 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl by number of atoms. How many ³⁷Cl atoms are present in 0.1 mol of chlorine atoms? (Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
questions.x: Total atoms = 0.1 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²²; a quarter of them are ³⁷Cl: 6.02 × 10²² × 0.25 = 1.505 × 10²². Using 75% gives 4.515 × 10²² (the ³⁵Cl atoms), and forgetting the abundance gives 6.02 × 10²².

questions.q: In the ionisation chamber of a mass spectrometer, atoms of the vaporised sample are usually turned into positive ions by:
o: Bombarding them with a beam of high-energy electrons
Passing them through a strong magnetic field
questions.x: A beam of fast electrons knocks an electron out of each atom, giving positive ions. The electric plates only accelerate the ions and the magnetic field only separates them; mixing up these stages gives the tempting wrong answers.

questions.q: Equal masses of H₂ and O₂ are placed in two separate flasks of equal volume at the same temperature. The ratio of pressures, P(H₂) : P(O₂), is: (H = 1, O = 16)
questions.x: At the same V and T, P ∝ n. For equal masses m, n(H₂) : n(O₂) = m/2 : m/32 = 16 : 1. 4 : 1 uses the square root as in Graham's law, and 1 : 16 inverts the ratio.

questions.q: Arrange ice, sodium, sodium chloride and quartz (SiO₂) in order of increasing melting point.
questions.x: Ice (molecular, hydrogen bonds) melts at 0 °C; sodium (weak metallic bonding, one electron per atom) at about 98 °C; NaCl (ionic) at about 801 °C; quartz (covalent network) above 1600 °C. Assuming every metal melts higher than an ionic solid puts sodium above NaCl.

questions.q: When the temperature of a liquid is raised, its surface tension:
questions.x: Faster-moving molecules weaken the effect of intermolecular attractions at the surface, so surface tension falls as temperature rises (as viscosity does).

questions.q: The maximum number of electrons that can occupy a subshell with azimuthal quantum number l = 3 is:
questions.x: l = 3 (an f subshell) has 2l + 1 = 7 orbitals (m = −3 to +3), each holding 2 electrons, so 14. 7 counts orbitals only; 6 and 10 are the p and d capacities.

questions.q: According to VSEPR theory, what is the shape of the methanal molecule, HCHO, in which carbon forms a double bond to oxygen and single bonds to two hydrogen atoms?
questions.x: Carbon has three electron regions (the C=O double bond counts as one) and no lone pair, so they point to the corners of a triangle: trigonal planar. Counting the double bond as two regions gives tetrahedral, the usual slip.

questions.q: For a process, ΔH is negative and ΔS is positive. Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, the process is:
questions.x: With ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, both terms make ΔG negative (−TΔS is negative for any T > 0), so ΔG < 0 at every temperature. 'Only at low temperatures' is the case for ΔH < 0 with ΔS < 0.

questions.q: Entropy is a measure of:
o: The heat content of a system at constant pressure
The degree of disorder or randomness of a system
The speed of a chemical reaction
The energy needed to start a reaction
questions.x: Entropy (S) measures disorder: the more ways the particles and their energy can be arranged, the higher the entropy. Heat content at constant pressure is enthalpy, the usual confusion.

questions.q: In the contact process, the mixture of SO₂ and air is purified and dried before it enters the converter. The main reason is that:
o: Impurities would shift the equilibrium to the left
Moist SO₂ is not oxidised at any temperature
Purification raises the temperature of the gases
Impurities such as arsenic compounds and dust would poison the catalyst
questions.x: Dust and impurities such as arsenic compounds settle on the catalyst surface and poison it, so the rate falls. Impurities do not change the position of equilibrium; that option confuses rate with yield.

questions.q: 0.20 mol of CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol of NaOH are dissolved together in water to make 1.0 dm³ of solution. What is the pH? (pKa of CH₃COOH = 4.74; log 2 = 0.30)
questions.x: NaOH neutralises 0.10 mol of the acid, leaving 0.10 mol CH₃COOH and forming 0.10 mol CH₃COO⁻: a buffer with equal amounts, so pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) = 4.74 + log 1 = 4.74. Using 0.10 salt and 0.20 acid without the reaction gives 4.44; inverting the ratio gives 5.04; 7.00 assumes complete neutralisation.

questions.q: When concentrated nitric acid is mixed with water, the mixture becomes hot and its volume is slightly less than the sum of the volumes mixed. Compared with the value predicted by Raoult's law, the vapour pressure of this mixture is:
o: Equal to the sum of the vapour pressures of the pure liquids
questions.x: Heat given out and a fall in volume show that the attractions between unlike molecules are stronger than in the pure liquids. Fewer molecules escape, so the vapour pressure is lower: a negative deviation. Higher would be the case for weaker unlike attractions.

questions.q: What is the average oxidation number of sulphur in sodium tetrathionate, Na₂S₄O₆?
questions.x: 2(+1) + 4x + 6(−2) = 0 gives 4x = 10, so x = +2.5 on average over the four sulphur atoms. Sharing the +10 between only two S atoms gives +5, and +6 is sulphur's value in sulphate, not here.

questions.q: The acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate, CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O → CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH, carried out in a large excess of water, follows first-order kinetics. It is called a pseudo-first-order reaction because:
o: Only one molecule takes part in the reaction
The acid catalyst is used up during the reaction
Water does not take part in the reaction
The concentration of water stays practically constant, so the rate depends only on [ester]
questions.x: Water is a reactant, but it is in such excess that its concentration hardly changes, so it is absorbed into the rate constant: rate = k′[ester]. The true reaction involves two molecules, so it only appears first order.

questions.q: A p-block element has electrons in five shells (n = 1 to 5) and three unpaired electrons in its ground state. What is its atomic number?
questions.x: Three unpaired p electrons means np³, here 5p³: [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5p³, Z = 36 + 10 + 2 + 3 = 51 (antimony). Forgetting the 4d¹⁰ gives 41; 33 has only four shells and 83 has six.

questions.q: 0.10 mol of calcium nitrate is heated strongly until it has decomposed completely, as other Group 2 nitrates do. What total volume of gas is given off, measured at STP? (molar volume 22.4 dm³)
questions.x: 2Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2CaO + 4NO₂ + O₂, so 0.10 mol gives 0.20 mol NO₂ and 0.05 mol O₂, a total of 0.25 mol = 0.25 × 22.4 = 5.6 dm³. Counting only NO₂ gives 4.48 dm³; counting only O₂ gives 1.12 dm³.

questions.q: 38.2 g of borax, Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O (molar mass 382 g mol⁻¹), is heated strongly until it forms a clear glass of NaBO₂ and B₂O₃. What is the mass of the glass? (H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: 0.10 mol borax loses 10 × 0.10 = 1.0 mol water (18.0 g), leaving 20.2 g of Na₂B₄O₇; the change Na₂B₄O₇ → 2NaBO₂ + B₂O₃ loses no mass, so the glass is 20.2 g. Giving the mass of water lost (18.0 g) instead of the residue is the most common slip.

questions.q: Sulphur dioxide is bubbled through acidified potassium dichromate solution. The colour change and the role of SO₂ are:
o: Green to orange; SO₂ is an oxidising agent
Orange to colourless; SO₂ is a bleaching agent only
Orange to yellow; SO₂ is a base
Orange to green; SO₂ is a reducing agent
questions.x: SO₂ (S +4) is oxidised to sulphate (+6) and reduces orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ (Cr +6) to green Cr³⁺. Reversing the colours treats SO₂ as the oxidant, the usual slip.

questions.q: In aqueous solution, the acid strength of the hydrogen halides increases in the order:
questions.x: Down the group the H–X bond gets longer and weaker, so it ionises more easily in water; HF is a weak acid and HI the strongest. Reversing the order by thinking the most electronegative halogen gives the strongest acid is the common slip.

questions.q: Vegetable oils are hydrogenated to make vegetable ghee using which catalyst?
questions.x: Hydrogen adds to the C=C bonds of the oil over finely divided nickel at about 150–200 °C. Promoted iron is the Haber process catalyst and V₂O₅ the contact process catalyst, the usual mix-ups.

questions.q: Bromoethane is warmed with aqueous NaOH: CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻. This reaction is classified as:
questions.x: The OH⁻ ion, an electron-pair donor, attacks the partly positive carbon of the C–Br bond and replaces Br⁻, so it is nucleophilic substitution. The reagent is a nucleophile, not an electrophile, and no double bond forms or is used.

questions.q: 2-Methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, reacts with HBr in the absence of peroxides. The intermediate formed in the first step is:
questions.x: H⁺ adds to the CH₂ end so that the positive charge sits on the carbon with three alkyl groups, the most stable carbocation; Br⁻ then gives 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (Markovnikov). The free radical belongs to the peroxide route, which is excluded here.

questions.q: Which reagent, used at room temperature, tells cyclohexene apart from benzene?
questions.x: Cyclohexene adds Br₂ and decolourises bromine water at once; benzene's delocalised ring does not add bromine under these conditions. Both compounds take up hydrogen over hot nickel and both burn, so those tests do not separate them, and neither reacts with aqueous NaOH.

questions.q: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, (CH₃)₂CBrCH₂CH₃, is heated with concentrated alcoholic KOH. The major organic product is:
questions.x: Alcoholic KOH with heat causes elimination. A β-H can go from a CH₃ (giving 2-methylbut-1-ene) or from the CH₂ (giving (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃); the more substituted alkene is the major product (Saytzeff rule). The alcohol would form with aqueous KOH; 3-methylbut-1-ene would need the double bond away from the C–Br carbon.

questions.q: Equal amounts of methanol, a primary, a secondary and a tertiary alcohol are added to sodium. The usual order of decreasing rate of hydrogen evolution is:
questions.x: Alkyl groups push electron density towards oxygen and make the O–H less acidic, and they also hinder solvation of the alkoxide ion, so acidity and the rate with sodium fall from CH₃OH to tertiary alcohols. The reversed order is the Lucas test order, which depends on carbocation stability.

questions.q: Propanone is warmed with iodine and aqueous NaOH: CH₃COCH₃ + 3I₂ + 4NaOH → CHI₃ + X + 3NaI + 3H₂O. The organic salt X is:
questions.x: The CH₃ of the CH₃CO– group becomes CI₃ and is split off as CHI₃; the rest of the molecule, CH₃CO–, becomes the ethanoate ion. So the salt has one carbon fewer than the ketone. Sodium propanoate forgets that a carbon leaves as iodoform.

questions.q: Sodium propanoate is (i) heated with soda lime to give gas X, and separately (ii) its concentrated aqueous solution is electrolysed (Kolbe's method) to give hydrocarbon Y at the anode. X and Y are:
questions.x: Soda lime removes CO₂: CH₃CH₂COONa + NaOH → CH₃CH₃ + Na₂CO₃, so X is ethane. In Kolbe electrolysis two CH₃CH₂COO⁻ ions each lose CO₂ and the two ethyl radicals join: Y is butane. Forgetting that the carboxyl carbon is lost gives propane and hexane.

questions.q: Which sequence converts propene into propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH?
o: HBr in the presence of a peroxide; then warm aqueous NaOH
HBr with no peroxide; then warm aqueous NaOH
questions.x: With a peroxide, HBr adds anti-Markovnikov to give 1-bromopropane, which aqueous NaOH hydrolyses to propan-1-ol. Without peroxide HBr adds by Markovnikov's rule (2-bromopropane), and acid-catalysed hydration also gives propan-2-ol; KMnO₄ gives a diol.

questions.q: An enzyme usually catalyses only one reaction or one type of substrate. This is mainly because:
o: Its active site has a shape that fits only particular substrate molecules
It raises the activation energy of all other reactions
It is used up in the reaction it catalyses
questions.x: Substrate and active site fit like a lock and key, held by specific interactions, so only matching molecules bind and react. Enzymes lower activation energy and are not consumed, so the other options contradict how catalysts work.

questions.q: Using ammonium sulphate, (NH₄)₂SO₄, as a fertiliser year after year tends to make the soil:
questions.x: NH₄⁺ ions are weakly acidic and are also turned into nitric acid by soil bacteria, and the sulphate stays behind, so the soil becomes acidic and may need lime. The fertiliser adds no potassium or phosphate.

questions.q: A CPU's address bus is made one line wider, from 16 lines to 17 lines. What happens to the number of memory locations it can address?
questions.x: With n address lines the CPU can address 2ⁿ locations, and 2¹⁷ = 2 × 2¹⁶, so the number doubles. Adding one line does not add one location; it adds a whole new bit position.

questions.q: The CPU needs a piece of data and does not find it in the cache. What happens next?
o: It stops the program with an error message
It reads the data from main memory, which takes longer
It reads the data from ROM instead
It waits until the data appears in the cache by itself
questions.x: A cache miss means the data is fetched from the slower main memory (RAM), and a copy is usually kept in cache for next time. It is not an error, and ROM does not hold the program's working data.

questions.q: Which statement about CD-R and CD-RW discs is correct?
o: A CD-R can be erased and rewritten; a CD-RW can be written only once
A CD-R can be written only once; a CD-RW can be erased and rewritten many times
Both can only be read, because both are kinds of CD-ROM
Both can be rewritten, but a CD-RW holds ten times more data
questions.x: R stands for recordable (write once, then read) and RW for rewritable (erase and write again). The swapped statement reverses the meanings of the two letters.

questions.q: The IPv4 address 127.0.0.1 (the loopback address) is used to:
o: Refer to the computer itself, for testing its own network software
Reach the main DNS server of the Internet
Send a message to every computer on the LAN
Connect directly to the ISP's router
questions.x: Packets sent to 127.0.0.1 never leave the computer; they loop back to it, which is useful for testing. A message to every computer on a LAN uses a broadcast address, not the loopback address.

questions.q: A network uses the subnet mask 255.255.255.192. How many addresses in each subnet can be given to hosts?
questions.x: 192 = 11000000, so the mask leaves 6 bits for hosts: 2⁶ = 64 addresses, minus the network address and the broadcast address, gives 62. 64 forgets to remove those two addresses.

questions.q: In a star network, the central switch stops working. What is the effect?
o: Only the computer nearest to the switch is affected
The computers pass data around in a ring instead
None of the computers can communicate through the network
Nothing changes, because each computer has its own cable
questions.x: In a star, all data between computers passes through the central device, so if it fails the whole network stops. Each computer having its own cable only protects the others when one cable, not the centre, fails.

questions.q: What is the safest place to download a new app for a smartphone?
o: A link received in an unknown SMS
A pop-up advertisement on a website
A file shared by an unknown chat group member
questions.x: Official app stores check apps before listing them, so the risk of malware is much lower. Links from unknown messages, pop-ups or strangers are common ways to spread malware.

questions.q: A website changes its PIN rule from 4 digits to 6 digits, each digit 0 to 9. By how many times does the number of possible PINs increase?
questions.x: 4 digits give 10⁴ = 10 000 PINs and 6 digits give 10⁶ = 1 000 000, and 1 000 000 ÷ 10 000 = 100. Two extra digits multiply the count by 10 each, not add 2.

questions.q: Managers in Lahore and Karachi hold a meeting in which they see and hear each other live over a network. This is:
questions.x: Video conferencing sends live video and sound between people in different places, saving travel. E-commerce is buying and selling online, not holding meetings.

questions.q: A new company uses cloud servers instead of buying its own. What is the main money advantage?
o: It never has to pay anything for computing
It owns the provider's servers after one year
It avoids a large cost for buying hardware at the start
It needs no staff who can use computers
questions.x: Renting cloud resources replaces a large upfront purchase with smaller payments for what is used. Cloud services are still paid for and remain the provider's property.

questions.q: A document contains the word Pakistan once. It is selected, Ctrl+X is pressed, and then Ctrl+V is pressed twice at the end of the document. How many times does Pakistan now appear?
questions.x: Ctrl+X removes the word and keeps it on the clipboard, and each Ctrl+V pastes one copy, so 0 + 2 = 2. The answer 3 treats Ctrl+X as if it were Ctrl+C, which would leave the original in place.

questions.q: A1 to A5 hold 4, 9, the text absent, 9 and 2. What does `=MAX(A1:A5)/COUNT(A1:A5)` show?
questions.x: `MAX` and `COUNT` both ignore the text: MAX = 9 and COUNT = 4 numbers, so 9 ÷ 4 = 2.25. 1.8 wrongly counts all 5 cells (9 ÷ 5).

questions.q: Staff(StaffID, Name, Dept, DeptPhone) repeats the department's phone number in every staff row. The Sales department has 6 staff. Its phone number changes. How many rows must be changed to keep the table correct?
questions.x: The number is stored once for each of the 6 Sales staff, so all 6 rows must be changed; changing fewer leaves an update anomaly. In a normalised design it would be stored once in a Department table.

questions.q: A hospital's rules: each doctor works in one department, and a department has many doctors; a doctor treats many patients, and a patient can be treated by many doctors. Which description of the relationships is correct?
questions.x: A department has many doctors but each doctor has one department, so that is one-to-many. Doctors and patients are "many" on both sides, so that is many-to-many.

questions.q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
In the design grid, "Maths" is typed under Subject and <500 under Price, both in the same Criteria row. Which titles are returned?
questions.x: Criteria in the same row are joined with AND, so a book must be Maths and cost under 500: Algebra 450 and Geometry 400. Reading them as OR would add Calculus and Atoms.

questions.q: A Fee field stores amounts in rupees and paisa, such as 1250.50, and is used in money calculations. Which Access data type suits it best?
questions.x: Currency is meant for money values and keeps them accurate in calculations. Short Text cannot be added or multiplied as numbers, and AutoNumber is filled in by Access itself.

questions.q: Which of these is a valid character constant in C?
questions.x: A character constant is one character in single quotes, 'k'. "k" is a string constant, k without quotes is an identifier, and 'k is missing its closing quote.

questions.q: A program compiles and links without errors. While it is running, the user enters 0, the program divides by this value and stops abnormally. What kind of error is this?
questions.x: The program was translated successfully and failed only while executing, so it is a run-time error. A syntax error would have been reported by the compiler before any executable was made.

Remainders are printed as they are found: 13 % 2 = 1 (n -> 6), 6 % 2 = 0 (n -> 3), 3 % 2 = 1 (n -> 1), 1 % 2 = 1 (n -> 0), giving 1011. That is the binary of 13 (1101) written backwards, because the lowest bit comes out first.
big returns the largest of its three arguments: big(7, 3, 11) = 11 and big(2, 9, 5) = 9, so 11 - 9 = 2.
The inner call show(3) runs first: it prints 3 and returns 6. The outer call show(6) prints 6 and returns 12, which goes into r and is printed last.

questions.q: What does `fclose(fp)` do?
o: Deletes the file from the disk
Writes any data still in the buffer to the file and releases the file
Erases all the data stored in the file
Moves to the start of the file so it can be read again
questions.x: fclose finishes work on a file: data waiting in the buffer is written out and the file is released. The file and its contents stay on the disk.

questions.q: An Agile team delivers 4 finished features at the end of every 2-week sprint. The product needs 18 features. At least how many weeks pass before all 18 are delivered?
questions.x: 18 / 4 = 4.5, and a part sprint still takes a whole sprint, so 5 sprints are needed: 5 x 2 = 10 weeks. 9 weeks treats 4.5 sprints as possible; 8 weeks (4 sprints) delivers only 16 features.
Slicing a tuple gives a tuple; `t[1:3]` takes indexes 1 and 2 (the end is excluded): (10, 15). `t[-1]` is the last item, 20. A tuple slice is printed with round brackets, not square ones.

questions.q: Which statement best describes inheritance?
o: One method name works in different ways for different classes
An object's data is hidden and reached only through its methods
A new class gets the attributes and methods of an existing class and can add its own
A program is broken into several unrelated functions
questions.x: Inheritance lets a child class reuse what its parent class defines and extend it. One method name behaving differently per class is polymorphism, and hiding data behind methods is encapsulation.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
d = {"Hamza": 70, "Iqra": 88}
print("Iqra" in d, 70 in d)
```
questions.x: `in` on a dictionary checks its keys only. "Iqra" is a key, so True; 70 is a value, not a key, so False.

questions.q: Which statement displays the word Hello on the screen in Python 3?
questions.x: In Python 3 `print` is a function, so its argument goes in brackets and the text in quotes. `printf` belongs to C, and `print Hello` without brackets is not valid Python 3.

questions.q: If someone found a polynomial-time algorithm for one NP-complete problem, what would follow?
o: Only that one problem would move into P
The halting problem would become solvable
Every problem in NP could be solved in polynomial time
Every NP-complete problem would become unsolvable
questions.x: Every NP problem reduces to any NP-complete problem in polynomial time, so a fast algorithm for one would give fast algorithms for all of NP (P = NP). The halting problem is unsolvable whatever happens to NP.

questions.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of bubble sort on n elements?
questions.x: In the worst case bubble sort makes about n passes of about n comparisons each, so O(n²). O(n log n) is merge sort's complexity.

questions.q: The mean of the four numbers 5, 8, x and 11 is 9. What is x?
questions.x: The four numbers must add up to 4 × 9 = 36; 5 + 8 + 11 = 24, so x = 36 − 24 = 12. 36 is the total, not the missing number.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly concerned with?
o: Why centring the clay is an essential first step in throwing a pot
How pots are fired and cooled in a kiln
Why beginners should not use a potter's wheel
How potters decorate the walls of a pot
questions.x: The passage says centring "decides whether everything that follows will succeed" and explains what goes wrong without it and how it is done. The kiln is mentioned only as a place where a badly centred pot may crack.

questions.q: According to the passage, why does a wobble grow if it is not corrected?
o: The wheel slows down as the clay dries
The clay becomes heavier on its low side
Water collects on one side of the lump
The high side is pushed harder each time it passes the fingers
questions.x: "Each time the high side passes the potter's fingers, it is pushed harder than the low side, so the wobble grows". Nothing is said about the wheel slowing down.

questions.q: The lesson that apprentices say "applies well beyond the wheel" is most likely that:
o: steady patience often achieves more than force
clay must always be kept wet
every task should be finished within one minute
skilled workers should not teach beginners
questions.x: The lesson is the one just described: beginners "fight the clay, gripping hard", while experienced potters "hold still and steady and let the clay come to them". The "first minute" in the opening describes how centring looks, not a rule.

questions.q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "true" most nearly means:
questions.x: Centring forces the clay "to run true", the opposite of the wobble described before: it turns evenly round the centre. "Honestly" is the word's common meaning, used of people and statements.

questions.q: What does the second paragraph mainly do?
o: It describes how a beginner learns to centre the clay
It explains what goes wrong if the clay is not centred
It gives the history of the potter's wheel
It shows how a pot is decorated before firing
questions.x: It describes a lump "even slightly off-centre" that wobbles and gives a pot uneven walls that "collapse" or "crack". How centring is done comes in the third paragraph.

questions.q: The writer's main purpose in the passage is to:
o: argue that quiet, empty moments can be valuable for creative thought
persuade teenagers to give up their phones completely
explain why waiting rooms make people uncomfortable
describe how earlier generations spent their free time
questions.x: The writer wants "to say a word in boredom's favour", calling it "the waiting room of imagination". Giving up phones is rejected: "None of this means we should ... throw away our phones".

questions.q: Where do many people say their best thoughts come to them?
o: In the shower or while on a long walk
While playing games on a phone
questions.x: The second paragraph says "their best thoughts arrive in the shower or on a long walk". Games and messages are what fill the quiet moments, which the writer sees as the problem.

questions.q: Which advice would the writer most likely give a student looking for fresh ideas for an essay?
o: Watch as many videos on the subject as possible
Spend some quiet time away from screens and let the mind wander
Give up using a phone for a whole year
Avoid walks so as not to waste study time
questions.x: The writer says a wandering mind "occasionally stumbles on an idea" and that a screen may fill "the very space in which original thought begins". A whole year without a phone goes far beyond the five minutes suggested.

questions.q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "fruitful" most nearly means:
questions.x: A long empty day can be "grim rather than fruitful", that is, unpleasant rather than producing good results such as ideas. "Full of fruit" is the literal meaning, which does not fit a day.

questions.q: In the third paragraph, the writer's attitude is best described as:
o: angry at people who use their phones
doubtful that boredom has any value
careful, limiting the claim so as not to overstate it
questions.x: The writer admits an empty day "can be grim" and distraction "can be a kindness", then says "My point is narrower". Enthusiasm for long empty days is the opposite of this caution.
